title: Coding agents access secrets through the CLI with piped stdin only; secret bytes never appear in a chat transcript, log line, or committed file
context: A coding agent that runs verbs, reads files, and captures its own tool output creates a large surface for secret material to land somewhere durable it should not be. Chat transcripts persist to model provider logs, session artefacts, and shared screenshots. Verbose tool logs land in the operator's terminal scrollback and in workspace backups. A `.env` file the agent generates in a scratch step ends up in git if a stray `git add` follows. The blueprint has to give agents an access path that is both usable (agents can wire the secret into the process that needs it) and safe (the bytes never traverse a surface the agent workflow persists).
decision: Agents work with secrets through the Secrets CLI (TAC-905) using piped-stdin flow-through, never argv, never terminal-echoed output. `secrets read N` is called with stdout piped to the downstream consumer (a process being started, a temp file being materialised into a container secret volume, a Kubernetes secret being created); the value crosses one pipe and no more. `secrets put N` is called with stdin piped from the source of the new value (a clipboard reader, another `secrets read` in a rotation flow, a hardware token flow). The CLI refuses to echo a value to a TTY without an explicit `--show` flag, and the flag is honoured only when stdout is actually a TTY (not a captured stream). The CLI's own log stream runs through a redactor that replaces any bytes matching a resolved secret value with a fixed placeholder before emitting. Agent-authored code and configuration never store a secret value as a literal, an inlined constant, or a comment; every reference is by logical name through the client.
consequences: Agent workflows compose secrets into running processes without the bytes crossing an observability surface the agent creates. The stdin-piped flow is unfamiliar to some tooling; projects wrap the pattern with small helper scripts (Node.js entry points that spawn a child process with the piped secret material as an environment variable set at spawn time and never printed) to keep the surface friendly. Human operators still have a debug path via `--show` on a real terminal, which is the one legitimate reason to look at a value with their own eyes. Nothing at this layer stops a human copying a value out of their own terminal; that class of leak requires an out-of-band delivery mode (see TAC-905 tradeoffs).

alternativesConsidered.name: Let the agent generate a `.env` file and reference it from process startup
alternativesConsidered.summary: The agent runs a reflector-like command that writes `.env` and the process reads from there.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: The `.env` file is now on disk with secret bytes for the lifetime of the working tree, and the agent's transcript of the reflector command already contains everything an attacker needs to reproduce it. A piped-stdin invocation crosses fewer boundaries and leaves nothing on disk unless the operator's own tooling asks for it (that path is the env reflector, deliberately per-invocation-per-operator, not per-agent-step).

alternativesConsidered.name: Provide agents a mock-value adapter that returns placeholders for every secret
alternativesConsidered.summary: The agent works against a stub vendor that always returns strings like `<REDACTED>` and the real values are injected later by a human.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: The stub adapter is a fine test-harness posture and does not need an ADR to authorise. It is not an access pattern for legitimate production wiring; the CLI's piped-stdin path is.
